points.heading: One-word verb times
points.body:
Today we learn how Spanish shows when an action happens. A verb is an action word, such as cantar, which means “to sing.” To conjugate means to change a verb for the person and the time. The indicative mood is used for facts that the speaker presents as real, such as «Yo canto» or «Ayer canté».

Simple tenses use one verb word. The present shows now or a habit: «canto». The imperfect shows a past action that was ongoing or repeated: «cantaba de niño». The preterite shows a finished past action: «canté ayer». The future looks ahead: «cantaré mañana». The conditional shows what would happen: «cantaría si pudiera». The stem is the part that stays, such as cant-, and the ending is the part that changes, such as -o or -é.

Read these forms as one small story: now I sing, before I used to sing, yesterday I sang, tomorrow I will sing, and in a possible situation I would sing.

Practice: Write the five “I” forms of cantar and then of comer. Next to each form, write when the action happens. Read them aloud in order.

Common mistake: Using «cantaba» for an event that is completely finished. For a closed yesterday event, Spanish usually uses «canté».

points.heading: Two-word verb times
points.body:
Sometimes Spanish uses two words. This is a compound tense. The first word is a helper form of haber, such as he, has, ha, había, habré, or habría. In these sentences, haber does not mean “there is.” The second word is the participle, the already-completed form of the verb: cantado, comido, or vivido.

Build «he cantado» slowly. He is the helper and cantado is the participle. Together they say that the action happened and matters now. The helper changes for the person, while the participle stays the same: «yo he cantado», «tú has cantado», and «ellos han cantado».

Practice: Write «he cantado», «había cantado», «habré cantado», and «habría cantado». Circle the helper and underline the participle. Then tell what time each helper shows.

Common mistake: Writing «hemos comidos». The helper changes, but the participle stays «comido»: «hemos comido».

points.heading: One word or two?
points.body:
Now we can choose between a simple form and a compound form. A simple form has one word, such as «terminé». A compound form has a helper and participle, such as «he terminado». First decide what your story needs to show.

Walk through three sentences. «Ayer terminé el libro» uses one word because yesterday is closed. «Ya he terminado el libro» uses two words because the result matters now. «Leía cuando sonó el teléfono» gives an ongoing background with leía and a finished event with sonó.

Practice: Write three pairs of sentences with the same verb. In each pair, use a one-word form and a two-word form. Explain what changes in the story.

Common mistake: Writing «Ayer he ido» for a trip that was finished yesterday. In that situation, use «Ayer fui».

lesson.summary: Indicative tenses tell when an action happens. Simple forms use one word, while compound forms join haber with a participle; choose them by the meaning of the story.
